title: Mapping Cones Cylinders and Chain Triangles

items.title: The mapping cone of a chain map
The mapping-cone differential squares to zero
items.strategy: Write the cone differential as a block matrix and multiply it by itself. The diagonal terms vanish because the source and target are complexes, and the mixed terms cancel exactly because the defining map is a chain map with the chosen minus sign on the shifted summand.

items.title: The canonical inclusion and projection for a mapping cone
The canonical mapping-cone sequence is degreewise split short exact
items.strategy: Check degree by degree that the canonical inclusion and projection are chain maps with zero composite. In each degree the cone is a direct sum of the target term and a shifted source term, so the displayed sequence is short exact and split as a sequence in the ambient abelian category even though the splittings need not commute with the differentials.

items.title: The cone triangle of a chain map
The cone of the zero map is the direct sum with a shift
items.strategy: Set the chain map equal to zero in the cone formula. The off-diagonal block disappears, so the differential is exactly the block-sum differential on the target complex together with the shifted source complex.

items.title: The cone of an identity map is contractible
items.strategy: Write the standard degree-one map that sends a cone term to the shifted source summand and check directly that d s + s d is the identity. The calculation uses only the cone differential and the identity map formula.

items.title: Isomorphic chain maps have isomorphic cones
items.strategy: Given a strictly commuting square with vertical chain isomorphisms, use the block-diagonal map on the two cone summands. The inverse is the corresponding block-diagonal map built from the inverse chain isomorphisms, and strict commutativity makes both maps chain maps.

items.title: A morphism of chain maps
A morphism of chain maps induces a chain map of cones
items.strategy: For a strictly commuting square, use the block-diagonal formula on the target and shifted-source summands. Expanding the two composites with the cone differentials shows the chain-map equation is exactly the commutativity of the given square.

items.title: Mapping cone is functorial on the arrow category of complexes
items.strategy: Identity squares give identity block maps and composing two strict squares composes the corresponding block maps. The cone construction therefore defines a functor on the arrow category of complexes, but only at that strict level.

items.title: Homotopic maps have chain-isomorphic mapping cones
items.strategy: If f - g = d s + s d, use the triangular matrix whose off-diagonal entry is the chosen homotopy s. Its inverse uses -s, and the homotopy equation is exactly what makes both matrices commute with the two cone differentials.

items.title: A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism exactly when its cone is acyclic
items.strategy: Start from the degreewise split short exact cone sequence and extract the exact four-term segment that compares H_n of the source, target, cone, and shifted source. The connecting map in that segment is the homology map induced by the original chain map, so vanishing of every cone homology object is equivalent to that map being an isomorphism in every degree.

items.title: A chain map is a homotopy equivalence exactly when its cone is contractible
items.strategy: Given a homotopy inverse and the two homotopies, package them into an explicit contracting homotopy for the cone. Conversely, start from a contracting homotopy on the cone, project its components onto the source and target summands, and read off a chain map in the opposite direction together with the two homotopies needed for a homotopy inverse.

items.title: The mapping cylinder of a chain map
The mapping-cylinder differential squares to zero
items.strategy: Multiply the block matrix for the cylinder differential by itself. The diagonal pieces vanish because the source and target are complexes, and the remaining mixed terms cancel because the displayed map is a chain map and the middle summand carries the compensating identity block.

items.title: The mapping cylinder factors a chain map
items.strategy: Use the explicit source inclusion, target inclusion, and projection coming from the direct-sum formula. The source inclusion is split degreewise by projection to the first summand, and the projection is a homotopy equivalence because the target inclusion is a section and the standard degree-one map gives the homotopy from the identity to the section-retraction composite.

items.title: The target is a strong deformation retract of the mapping cylinder
items.strategy: Keep the explicit target inclusion and projection from the factorization theorem and check that the standard homotopy from the identity to the section-retraction composite vanishes on the target summand. That is the chain-level deformation-retract statement relative to the target.

items.title: Every chain map factors as a cofibration-like inclusion followed by a homotopy equivalence
items.strategy: Apply the mapping-cylinder factorization theorem and retain only the two structural conclusions it already proved: a degreewise split monomorphism followed by a chain-homotopy equivalence.

items.title: The quotient of the mapping cylinder by its source is the mapping cone
items.strategy: Take the cokernel of the source inclusion degreewise and identify the quotient with the target summand together with the shifted source summand. Under that identification the induced differential is exactly the cone differential.

items.title: Cones preserve chain-homotopy equivalences of arrows
items.strategy: Use the chosen homotopy-commuting square to write the usual upper-triangular cone map and do the same for the chosen homotopy inverse square. The inverse data and the comparison homotopies assemble into a homotopy inverse for the induced cone map.

items.title: The three-cone calculation for a composite chain map
items.strategy: For a composite C -> D -> E, write the evident maps between Cone(f), Cone(g f), and Cone(g) in block form. Then identify the cone of the first of those maps with a complex that is blockwise isomorphic, and hence homotopy equivalent, to Cone(g) by an explicit change of coordinates.

items.title: The cone triangle of a null-homotopic map splits in the homotopy category
items.strategy: A null-homotopic map is homotopic to the zero map, so the previous cone-isomorphism lemma identifies its cone with the cone of zero. The zero-map cone is the direct sum of the target and the shifted source, which is exactly the splitting data in the additive homotopy category.

items.title: A chain map with contractible cone becomes an isomorphism in the homotopy category
items.strategy: In the homotopy category, isomorphisms are exactly chain-homotopy equivalences. Apply the cone criterion for homotopy equivalence and reinterpret its conclusion in K(A).

items.title: The cone construction commutes with shift up to the canonical sign isomorphism
items.strategy: Compare the shifted cone differential with the cone differential of the shifted map. The two formulas differ only by the sign placed on the shifted source summand, so multiplying that summand by the canonical sign gives an isomorphism of complexes.

items.title: An exact functor carries mapping-cone sequences to mapping-cone sequences
items.strategy: An exact functor between abelian categories is additive, so it preserves zero objects, finite biproducts, and the degreewise chain-map formulas. Applying the functor degreewise to the cone construction therefore produces the cone of the induced chain map, together with the transported canonical inclusion and projection.

items.title: The relative homology of a chain map
Relative homology is invariant under homotopy equivalence of arrows
items.strategy: A homotopy equivalence of arrows induces a chain-homotopy equivalence of cones. Homotopy equivalences are quasi-isomorphisms, so the induced map on homology identifies the relative homology objects.

items.title: Relative homology vanishes exactly for quasi-isomorphisms
items.strategy: By definition the relative homology of a map is the homology of its cone. Therefore it vanishes in every degree exactly when the cone is acyclic, and the cone criterion translates that directly into the quasi-isomorphism condition.

items.title: FALSE: the mapping-cone differential needs no minus sign
items.strategy: Replace the cone differential by the naive unsigned block matrix and square it. The mixed term survives with the wrong sign, so the result need not be zero even when the original map is a chain map.

items.title: FALSE: the degreewise splitting of the cone sequence is a chain splitting
items.strategy: A degreewise direct-sum decomposition does not force the chosen section and retraction to commute with the differentials. For the identity map on a stalk complex the cone sequence is degreewise split, but any chain splitting would make the comparison with the shifted homology to vanish, which fails for the identity map.

items.title: FALSE: mapping cone is a functor on the homotopy category with no extra data
items.strategy: Strict commutative squares give a genuine functor on the arrow category, but homotopy-commuting squares require a chosen homotopy and different choices generally change the induced cone map. What survives without extra data is only noncanonical isomorphism of cones in the homotopy category.

items.title: FALSE: an acyclic mapping cone is contractible
items.strategy: Take an acyclic but noncontractible complex and map it by zero to the zero complex. Its cone is just the shift of that acyclic complex, so it is acyclic but still not contractible, showing that quasi-isomorphism is weaker than chain-homotopy equivalence.

items.title: FALSE: the mapping-cylinder factorization is a model-category factorization
items.strategy: This page proves only a chain-level factorization into a degreewise split monomorphism and a homotopy equivalence. A model-category factorization would additionally require a specified model structure and lifting axioms, none of which has been defined here.

title: Mapping Cones Cylinders and Chain Triangles — Examples

items.title: The cone of multiplication by m on the integers
items.strategy: View multiplication by m as a chain map between stalk complexes concentrated in degree 0. The cone then has Z in degrees 0 and -1 with differential multiplication by m, so its homology reads off ker(m) and coker(m) directly.

items.title: The cone of zero and of the identity
items.strategy: Compute the cone of the zero map and of the identity map on a stalk complex. The zero-map cone is just a shift, while the identity cone carries the explicit contraction from the main theorem.

items.title: A quasi-isomorphism detected by an acyclic cone
items.strategy: Use the identity map on a stalk complex. Its cone is contractible, hence acyclic, so the cone criterion recognizes the map as a quasi-isomorphism in the most explicit possible case.

items.title: An acyclic noncontractible cone
items.strategy: Take the three-term complex attached to a concrete nonsplit short exact sequence of abelian groups, for example 0 -> Z --2-> Z -> Z/2 -> 0, and map it by zero to the zero complex. Its cone is just the shift of that acyclic but noncontractible complex, so the cone is again acyclic and still not contractible.

items.title: The mapping cylinder of an inclusion of two-term complexes
items.strategy: Take a simple inclusion of two-term complexes in abelian groups and write out the cylinder term by term. The example makes the source inclusion, target inclusion, projection, and deformation retraction completely concrete.

items.title: Relative homology of a map between stalk complexes
items.strategy: Reuse the stalk-complex computation for multiplication by m. The relative homology is the homology of the cone, so one sees directly that H_0 is the cokernel and H_-1 is the kernel of the underlying homomorphism.

items.title: The three-cone calculation for a composite
items.strategy: Take two composable multiplication maps between stalk complexes and compute the three relevant cones explicitly. The displayed matrices make the comparison maps and the resulting homotopy equivalence visible on the nose.

items.title: A degreewise split cone sequence with no chain splitting
items.strategy: Use the identity map on the stalk complex Z[0]. The canonical cone sequence is degreewise split because every term is a direct sum, but any chain splitting would force the comparison with the shifted homology to vanish, which fails for the identity map.
